newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan set for WTO, aviation talks with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Taiwan set for WTO, aviation talks with U.S..

text.p: Taiwan was preparing to host a new round of talks with the United States on Thursday on the island's bid to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), Taiwan officials said.
The sides also planned to hold talks in late February in Washington on revisions to a bilateral aviation agreement, officials said.

"The four-day entry bid talks which begin tomorrow (Thursday) in Taipei will focus on market access for liquor and cigarettes, agriculture, services and government purchase issues," a Board of Foreign Trade spokesman told Reuters.
Lin Yi-fu, head of the cabinet-level board, will be Taiwan's chief negotiator. His U.S. counterpart is David Burns, who oversees Taiwan affairs under the U.S. Trade Representative.
The sides also would discuss general economic issues, the spokesman said.
Taiwan has no formal ties with the United States, which recognises only Beijing's communist government, but has extensive commercial ties with Washington.

The last round of talks, held in Taipei in mid-November, ended without significant agreements, as the sides differed on how much Taiwan should liberalise its agricultural, tobacco and alcohol industries.

Taiwan currently runs a monopoly on the domestic tobacco and alcohol markets, with importers obliged to pay stiff monopoly fees, and subsidises many farm products by setting government-guaranteed prices.
Taiwan, keen to join the WTO in 1997, has completed necessary bilateral talks with 12 of the 26 WTO members that have sought such dialogue with Taipei.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join the organisation's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.

Taiwan's scheduled February 26-27 talks with U.S. officials in Washington will focus on increasing of Taiwan's commercial flights to the United States and onward extension of these flights to third countries, aviation officials said.

Taiwan's China Airlines and EVA Airways, a unit of shipping giant Evergreen Marine, now are allowed to serve seven U.S. cities and extend such flights to one European country and one central American country.

Taiwan officials said Washington agreed to hold the talks because it hoped Taiwan could sign the U.S.-sponsored open-skies agreement that allows supporting airlines to fly without restrictions to and beyond each other's boundaries.
